chapters.title: Chapter 4: Cost Advantages, Scale, and Distribution

lessons.title: Distribution Reach as a Competitive Advantage

body.text: A product nobody can find is a product nobody buys. In India, getting onto the shelf of a crore small shops is so hard and so expensive that doing it well is a moat on its own.

children.text: India's retail landscape is unusually fragmented. Most everyday goods are still bought from small neighbourhood kirana stores, chemists, paint dealers, and hardware shops spread across cities, towns, and villages. For a manufacturer, reaching them means building a network of distributors, stockists, delivery routes, and salespeople that can take decades. A company that has already built it can launch a new product into lakhs of outlets almost overnight. A challenger cannot.
Where Distribution Becomes a Moat

body.caption: Distribution advantages across Indian listed companies

cells: Distributors and delivery routes reaching lakhs of small outlets directly, including in rural India
Hindustan Unilever, Dabur, and Marico, with some of the widest outlet reach in the country
Dealer network with in-store tinting machines and frequent replenishment, so dealers carry less stock and still never run out
Asian Paints, which built its dealer supply chain over decades
Deep presence in small hardware shops plus relationships with carpenters, plumbers, and contractors
Dealers and service centres in small towns, so buyers know they can get servicing nearby
Hero MotoCorp in rural two-wheelers; Maruti Suzuki's sales and service network
Bank branches used to sell insurance and mutual funds to existing customers
SBI Life Insurance and SBI Funds Management, drawing on SBI's very large branch network

children.text: The Economics of a Delivery Route

markDefs.definition: The average value of goods sold to a retailer in one delivery or sales visit. A larger drop size spreads the fixed cost of the visit over more sales.

children.text: The cost of distribution is mostly fixed per route: a van, a driver, a salesperson, fuel. What changes is how much the company sells on each visit, called the
drop size
. A company with dozens of fast-moving products sells much more per visit than a company with a handful.

body.latex: \text{Distribution cost as \% of sales} = \frac{\text{Monthly route cost}}{\text{Visits per month} \times \text{Average drop size}} \times 100

children.text: Worked Example: The Same Route, Two Companies

A route costs ₹60,000 a month. The van covers 30 outlets a day for 26 days, so 780 visits a month. The large FMCG company has a broad portfolio and sells ₹2,000 per visit on average. The challenger has three products and sells ₹400 per visit.

body.caption: Monthly economics of one delivery route

body.title: Distribution Cost as % of Sales on the Same Route

children.text: The challenger pays five times as much, as a share of sales, to reach exactly the same shops. It can either charge more, accept thin or negative margins, or reach far fewer outlets by using wholesalers instead of direct routes. Every option leaves it weaker. That is why challenger brands in India often stay regional for years.

body.title: Help the Challenger
body.prompt: The challenger adds two new products and doubles its average drop size to ₹800. With the same route cost of ₹60,000 and 780 visits a month, what is its distribution cost as a percentage of sales?
body.explanation: Monthly sales = 780 × ₹800 = ₹6,24,000. Distribution cost = ₹60,000 ÷ ₹6,24,000 × 100 = 9.6%. Much better than 19.2%, but still more than double the large company's 3.8%. Breadth of portfolio and depth of distribution reinforce each other.

body.text: Distribution moats are self-reinforcing. A wide network makes new product launches cheap, which widens the portfolio, which raises drop size, which makes the network even cheaper per rupee of sales. A challenger has to break into this loop with one product at a time.

children.text: Why Retailers and Dealers Prefer the Leader
Fast-moving stock:
shelf space in a small shop is scarce. Products that sell quickly earn the shopkeeper more per square foot.
Reliable replenishment:
frequent deliveries let the shop hold less inventory and tie up less cash.
Customer pull:
customers ask for well-known products by name, and a shop that does not stock them loses the sale.
Schemes and relationships:
leaders run trade schemes, dealer meets, and loyalty programmes for retailers and influencers that smaller rivals cannot afford at the same scale.
Spotting Distribution Strength in the Numbers

markDefs.definition: The average number of days a company takes to collect payment from customers: trade receivables ÷ sales × 365. Low debtor days suggest strong bargaining power over distributors and dealers.

children.text: The clearest financial signal of distribution power is how quickly dealers and distributors pay. A company that dealers need can insist on advance payment or short credit periods. Check
debtor days
in the Ratios section on Screener.in.

body.label: The distribution power signal
body.value: Low and stable debtor days alongside steady sales growth
body.context: If a company must extend longer credit to distributors to keep growing, it is pushing stock into the channel, not being pulled by demand.

children.text: Low or negative working capital, meaning dealers and distributors effectively help finance the business.
Direct outlet reach numbers disclosed in annual reports and investor presentations, and whether they are growing, especially in rural areas.
New product launches that scale quickly, a sign the network can carry them.
Stable margins despite regional challengers, showing the network keeps competitors at bay.
How Digital Channels Are Changing the Game

body.title: Traditional distribution moat vs the digital challenge

columns.label: Where the moat still holds
points: Rural and small-town India, still dominated by kirana stores
Bulky or technical products needing dealer advice, such as paints and building materials
Categories needing service networks, such as vehicles
Products where retailer recommendation drives the choice
Distribution scale that also wins the best placement on quick commerce apps

columns.label: Where it is being bypassed
points: Urban shoppers buying through e-commerce and quick commerce apps
Digital-first brands reaching customers directly online
Retail chains and apps promoting their own private labels
Online search replacing the shelf as the place products are discovered
Lower cost for a new brand to reach metro customers nationally

children.text: Quick commerce and e-commerce let a new brand reach customers in metro cities without building a single delivery route. That lowers the barrier in urban India, particularly for premium and niche products. But the advantage cuts both ways: established brands with the strongest demand also tend to win visibility on these apps. The distribution moat is shrinking in metros and holding in the rest of the country.

body.title: Which Distribution Moat Is Most Durable?
body.question: Which company's distribution advantage is least likely to be bypassed by quick commerce and e-commerce?
options: A premium skincare brand sold mainly in metro cities
A snack brand whose sales come mostly from urban modern trade
A paint company whose products are tinted at dealer shops and chosen with painter and contractor advice across small towns
A digital-first apparel brand sold only online
body.explanation: Paints depend on dealer tinting, contractor advice, and small-town reach, which apps cannot easily replace. Metro premium skincare and urban snacks are exactly where online channels are growing fastest. A digital-first brand has no physical distribution moat at all.

body.title: The Quick Commerce Challenger
body.scenario: A listed FMCG company has sold packaged spices through a network reaching about 8 lakh outlets for 30 years, with debtor days under 15. Its metro sales growth has slowed to 3% while a digital-first spice brand, sold mainly on quick commerce apps in eight cities, is growing at 60% a year. The incumbent's rural and small-town sales are still growing at 9%.
body.prompt: Is the incumbent's distribution moat broken? How should an investor think about this?
body.modelAnswer: The moat is not broken, but it is narrowing in part of the market. In metros, quick commerce lets the digital-first brand reach customers without building routes, so the incumbent's network matters less there, which is showing up as slower metro growth. In rural and small-town India, the incumbent's reach is still an advantage the challenger cannot match, which is why growth there remains healthy. Debtor days under 15 suggest distributors still value the product. An investor should split the business: what share of sales comes from metros versus the rest, and how fast each is growing; whether the incumbent is gaining visibility and share on quick commerce apps itself, using its brand strength; gross margins, to see whether it is discounting to defend metro share; and whether the challenger expands beyond metros, which would require the costly offline distribution it has so far avoided. If rural growth holds and the incumbent adapts online, the overall moat stays largely intact.

body.title: Check a Company's Distribution Strength
steps: Pick a listed consumer or building materials company you follow
On Screener.in, note debtor days for the last 10 years from the Ratios section
Check working capital days or cash conversion cycle for the same period
Find outlet reach or dealer count in the latest annual report or investor presentation
Read the latest concall for comments on rural versus urban growth and on quick commerce
Decide whether its distribution advantage is widening, stable, or narrowing

body.text: Companies named are used to illustrate concepts from public information and are not investment recommendations. Route economics, outlet numbers, and the spice company scenario are hypothetical.

points: India's fragmented retail makes wide distribution slow and expensive to build, so an established network can be a moat on its own
Distribution cost is largely fixed per route, so companies with broad portfolios and larger drop sizes reach the same shops far more cheaply
Distribution moats are self-reinforcing: reach makes launches cheap, launches widen the portfolio, and a wider portfolio raises drop size
Low, stable debtor days and low working capital signal that dealers need the company more than it needs them
Quick commerce and e-commerce are weakening distribution moats in metros, especially for premium and niche products
Distribution advantages remain strong in rural and small-town India, and in categories needing dealer advice or service
